parole.testo: Inherited from Danish ansigt, from Middle Low German ansicht. By surface analysis, an- + sikt, literally “on-sight”. Displaced native Norwegian Bokmål andlet (“face”). Compare Swedish ansikte, and further German Ansicht (“view”) and Angesicht (“face”).
From Danish afhandling, from the verb afhandle; originally from Middle Low German or Low German.
From Danish afslutte, a compound word of av- + slutte (“close, conclude, finish”), probably a loan-translation from Middle Low German (compare with German abschließen). Compare to Swedish avsluta.

parole.significato: to begin, start (initiate or take the first step into something.)
parole.testo: From Danish begynde, from Middle Low German beginnen, cognate with Old English beginnan (English begin), from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną. Displaced native Norwegian børje (“to begin, start”), from Old Norse byrja, compare Norwegian Nynorsk byrja and Swedish börja.

Inherited from Danish betyde, formed after Middle Low German bedü̂den (compare German bedeuten). By surface analysis, be- + ty(de). The contracted pronunciation is probably due to native Norwegian influence as it seems not to have been common in Danish; compare by.

Inherited from Danish billede, from Old Danish beletæ, from Middle Low German bēl(e)de, from Old Saxon bilithi, from Proto-West Germanic *biliþi. The contracted spelling was first standardized in 1938.

Short form of blive, from Danish blive, from Middle Low German bliven. Meanings 2, 3 and 4 are taken from Old Norse verða, which also has given rise to the dated vorde. In several dialects, the Low German word did not displace the Old Norse word completely. As a result, vart was allowed in past tens
From the expression blive på sjøen (literally “to remain at sea”). Thus the same word as bli (“to remain, become”), from Danish blive, from Middle Low German blîven, from Proto-Germanic *bilībaną.

parole.significato: to break, snap (turn into two or more pieces)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish brække, from Middle Low German brēken, from Old Saxon brekan, from Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”). In older Danish, the verb had both strong and weak conjugation. While contemporary Danish has generalized the weak forms, Bokmål has followed the opposite tendency.
From Danish brændevin, a calque of Middle Low German bernewin.
From Danish feje, from Middle Low German vēgen, from Proto-West Germanic *fegōn.
Inherited from Danish fætter (older fædder), from Middle Low German vedder. Compare German Vetter.

Inherited from Danish fire, from Middle Low German vîren, from Old French virer, of uncertain origin, but probably from Latin vībrare. If so, a doublet of vibrere. Cognate with English veer, which compare.
Inherited from Danish forbause (now spelt forbavse), from Middle Low German vorbāsen, whence also German verbaseln. Further cognate with Dutch verbazen.

parole.significato: to be in charge of, direct, manage
parole.testo: fore- + stå, same as Danish forestå, from older Danish forestaa, forstaa, forstande, from Middle Low German vorstān
Inherited from Danish foretage, from Middle Low German vornemen. fore- + ta. Cf. Swedish företa and German vornehmen.
From Danish hvordan, from Old Danish hurædan, from Middle Low German wōdān, from wo (“how”) + doon (“do”). Equivalent to German wo (“where”) + tun (“do”).
Inherited from Danish håbe with native Norwegian -p-, from Middle Low German hōpen, from Proto-West Germanic *hopōn, which see for cognates. Further origin uncertain.

parole.significato: to treat others to food and drink, especially when being admitted to an association or starting at a new workplace
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish hønse, corresponding to Swedish hönsa, ultimately from Middle Low German hensen (“to admit into an association; to pay to be admitted into an association”), derived from hanse (“Hanse, guild, association”).
Inherited from Danish kikke, kigge, from Middle Low German kîken.

Inherited from Danish krønike, from Middle Low German kröneke ~ kroneke, from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “relating to time”), derived from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). Compare Swedish krönika and see there for notes on the umlaut vowel.

parole.significato: a container, originally woven and often having a handle, used to carry or store things; a basket
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish kurv, from Old Danish korw, itself borrowed from Middle Low German korf, from Old Saxon *korf, from Proto-West Germanic *korb. The further origin is uncertain; a traditional connection with Latin corbis (“basket”) is disputed. The basketball sense is a semantic loan from English
Inherited from Danish kvæde, from Middle Low German quēde, from Old Saxon *quidina, from Latin cydōnia.
From Danish kyndig, from Middle Low German kundich.
From Danish lække, from Middle Low German lecken. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk leka and English leak. The past form lakk is from oral Norwegian, compare to Nynorsk lak.
From Danish lykke, from Middle Low German lucke, gelucke.

parole.significato: a mixture of finely minced pork and added fat, used especially to make patties and sausages
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish medister, from Middle Low German metworst (“sausage made from minced pork”), remodelled under the influence of ister (“suet, visceral fat”). The Middle Low German compound consists of met (“pork”) and worst (“sausage”). The first element ultimately derives from Proto-Germanic *m

parole.significato: a fried patty of seasoned, finely minced pork with a relatively high fat content
parole.testo: From medister (“minced pork mixed with fat”) + kake (“cake; patty”), literally “medister patty”. The first element medister was borrowed through Danish medister, an alteration of Middle Low German metworst (“sausage made from minced pork”), influenced by ister (“suet, visceral fat”). The first eleme
Inherited from Danish mægtig, from Middle Low German mechtich, from Old Saxon mahtig, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mahtīgaz. Compare Swedish mäktig.

parole.significato: but, however, though introducing a clause that contrasts with the preceding clause or sentence
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish men, from Middle Low German man, men (“only, but”), partially merged with Old Norse meðan (“while”), whence Bokmål mens.

parole.significato: to stare open-mouthed; to be agape in wonder, astonishment, confusion, surprise, and/or flabergastation
parole.testo: From Danish måbe, from Middle Low German mopen.
From Danish nidkær, from obsolete nidkærlighed, derived from Middle Low German nidige leve.
From obsolete oppstudsig and older Danish, after Middle Low German upstutzig.

parole.significato: old liquid measure equivalent to 241 ml
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish pægl (pronounced /pɛl/), from Middle Low German pēgel. Compare German Pegel (“gauge, water level”).

Via Danish regne from Middle Low German rekenen, from Proto-Germanic *rekanōną. Cognate with English reckon, German rechnen, and Dutch rekenen. Icelandic reikna, Norwegian Nynorsk rekna, and Swedish räkna are also borrowed from Low German.

parole.significato: seal (impression in wax etc. on a document as a symbol of authenticity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish segl, from Middle Low German sēgel, from Proto-West Germanic *sigil, from Latin sigillum.
From Danish sikker, from Middle Low German seker, from Latin sēcūrus “secure, unworried”.
Inherited from Danish slæbe with native Norwegian -p-, from Middle Low German slêpen, from Proto-West Germanic *slaipijan. Doublet of sløyfe (“to strike, omit”).

parole.significato: to cut out, leave out, omit, skip
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish sløjfe, from Middle Low German sloifen, sleifen (“to raze, tear down”), itself borrowed from Middle High German sleifen, from Proto-West Germanic *slaipijan. Cognate with native Middle Low German slêpen, whence the Norwegian doublet slepe (“to drag”). Compare German schleifen a
From Danish spise, or directly from Middle Low German spīse, from Old Saxon spīsa, from Latin expensa (noun; Late Latin form spēsa). Cognates include German Speise and German speisen.

parole.significato: to enter into / upon, take over or take up (a position), step into, embark upon, start (a journey)
parole.testo: From older tiltrede, probably from Danish tiltræde, from Middle Low German treden.
From Danish tragt, from Middle Low German trechtäre, trechter, from Old Saxon trahtari, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtārī, from Late Latin tractārius, from Latin trāiectōrium.

parole.significato: science, scholarly knowledge, scholarship (collective discipline of learning acquired through any scholarly method; tot…
parole.testo: From viten (“knowledge”) + -skap (“-ship”). Structurally inherited from Danish videnskab, itself after Middle Low German wētenschap (cf. German Wissenschaft). The form with ⟨t⟩ was formed by Knudsen after the underlying verb vite (“to know”), according to his general policy of avoiding inconsistenci

parole.significato: moment, blink of an eye (short but unspecified period of time)
parole.testo: Inherited from Danish øjeblik, a partial calque of Middle Low German ôgenblick. By surface analysis, øye (“eye”) + blikk (“glance”). Compare German Augenblick etc.
